extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and policymakers interested in lobbying and its regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of legal, ethical and procedural standards, disclosure requirements, and institutional practices used to regulate lobbying across jurisdictions (EU, US, UK, Germany, Italy, India, New Zealand, etc.). Focuses on registers, codes of conduct, cooling-off rules, definitions, and transparency measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: MEPs must publish meetings with interest representatives (EU amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment to the European Parliament's Rules of Procedure: 'rapporteurs, shadow rapporteurs or committee chairs shall, for each report, publish online all scheduled meetings with interest representatives falling under the scope of the Transparency Register.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a binding rule adopted 31 January 2019 to increase transparency of contacts between Members of the European Parliament and lobbyists; applies to meetings related to drafting and negotiating legislation and references the EU Transparency Register as the scope-defining database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency Register (EU)
rubrics_metrics.description: A database of lobbyists (the Transparency Register) used by the EU to record interest representatives and their interactions with EU institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Register is used to define the scope of transparency obligations (e.g., which interest representatives trigger MEPs' meeting-publication duties). The page notes broad participation (consultants, associations, corporations, NGOs) and that the register is central to EU transparency reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory lobby registers / public registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement that lobbyists and/or lobbying firms be listed on a public register (examples: Germany introduced a mandatory lobby register effective 1 January 2022; some Italian regions and various Australian states have registers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts jurisdictions with mandatory registers (Germany) against those without (France, India, New Zealand), and notes subnational registers (six Italian regions, Australian state registers) and the role of registers in transparency and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of conduct for lobbyists
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal code of conduct governing lobbyists' behaviour; in some places non-binding, in others combined with registers and binding rules (Germany introduced a code alongside its register).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codes can be non-binding (earlier EU practice) or binding; the page notes moves from voluntary codes toward binding transparency/ethics rules (e.g., EU amendments, Germany's law) and that critics sometimes find codes insufficient without enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling-off periods and revolving-door restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that prevent or limit former public officials from immediately becoming lobbyists or from lobbying their former institutions for a defined period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page documents the 'revolving door' phenomenon and recommends stronger ethics frameworks (including independent ethics bodies and longer cooling-off periods for MEPs). Examples: Transparency International data on ex-MEPs and Commissioners entering lobbying; New Zealand's Immigration Advisers Licensing Act (one-year restriction for certain immigration officials) as an ad hoc cooling-off provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration as a foreign agent (FARA) for foreign lobbying in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, entities lobbying on behalf of foreign governments or principals must register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that foreign-funded lobbying is legal but requires FARA registration; gives examples of foreign-state-funded lobbying and enforcement cases (e.g., failures to register have led to prosecutions or guilty pleas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-employment and administration official bans (executive orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive-order-style bans on former administration officials lobbying for foreign governments or other restricted lobbying activities (example: a Trump order creating lifetime and five-year bans, later revoked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such bans are used to limit conflicts of interest but can be temporary or revoked; the article cites Trump-era measures (lifetime ban on lobbying for foreign governments for administration officials, five-year ban for others) and notes revocation near the end of that presidency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory disclosure of lobbying activities, clients and spending
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements that lobbyists, lobbying firms, or employers disclose information about their clients, lobbying activities and spending (examples include US Lobbying Disclosure Act filings, studies citing spending statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references reporting regimes and research that depend on disclosures (LDA thresholds and filings, FARA disclosures). It also cites empirical studies and figures on lobbying expenditures, demonstrating why financial disclosure is a central transparency tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition of 'lobbying' and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal definitions to determine what activity counts as lobbying (example: UK Public Affairs Council definition quoted: professional attempts to influence government, parliament or public bodies; distinguishes public individual lobbying from corporate/association lobbying).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise legal/administrative definitions are essential because they determine who must register or disclose; definitions often exclude casual constituent contact and focus on organized/professional influence activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry/substantive exceptions and sector-specific rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Special rules or exceptions for particular sectors or activities (examples: immigration advisers' one-year restriction in New Zealand; sector lobbying norms in India where industry bodies engage ahead of budgets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations often include tailored provisions for specific industries or professions, reflecting different risks (e.g., immigration advising, defence, energy), and may be implemented at national or sectoral levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, enforcement and independent oversight (ethics bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment of independent ethics bodies or enforcement mechanisms to address conflicts of interest, failures to disclose, or improper influence; the page argues stronger ethics frameworks could avoid conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency International and others recommend independent oversight and enforceable sanctions (longer cooling-off periods, monitoring ex-officials' career moves); criticisms of some laws (e.g., Germany's initially criticized rules) highlight the need for enforcement capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-procurement and public-procedure transparency (preventing favouritism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for impartial, transparent public procedures (example: EU directive leading to abolition of old Italian concession rule and later mandated public procedures to avoid favouritism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article cites the 2006 EU directive requiring mandatory public procedures for concessions, and the Italian debate over beach concessions as an example where lack of transparent procedure enabled lobbying to preserve privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization or prohibition of lobbying in certain jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries lobbying is illegal or widely treated as corruption (example: South Korea views lobbying as a form of corruption and it is illegal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal regimes vary: some countries criminalize certain lobbying practices or view them as corrupt, while others regulate through registration and disclosure; enforcement and cultural attitudes shape these distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for NGO neutrality and funding disclosure (UN/NGO consultative status risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations that NGOs, particularly those with UN consultative status, maintain neutrality and disclose funding sources to avoid being influenced by state actors (examples: allegations against RADDHO and TACUDU accepting UAE funds and calls to suspend consultative status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses cases where NGOs took large sums from state-linked sources to advance geopolitical agendas as evidence for stronger transparency and possible sanctions (suspension of consultative status) to protect institutional integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration thresholds and scope under national disclosure laws (e.g., LDA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal thresholds that determine when employers or firms must register or report lobbying activity (example: references to Lobbying Disclosure Act threshold changes and debate on registration thresholds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds decide which expenditures or activities trigger reporting; changes or increases in thresholds (cited updates to LDA thresholds) can significantly affect transparency and coverage of lobby disclosure regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and ethics as antidotes to democratic deficit and agent misdirection
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative standard: lobbying laws and practices should minimize conflicts of interest and agent misdirection (the failure of officials to serve public interest because of private influence), thereby reducing democratic deficit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents critiques of lobbying that emphasize the need for transparency, accountability, and limits on special-interest influence to preserve democratic responsiveness and prevent elected officials from shifting away from the median voter due to special-interest money.
